title: Pool Terms Every Beginner Should Know: A Plain-English Billiards Glossary
description: Rack, bank, English, safety, on the hill: a friendly glossary of the pool and billiards terms every beginner hears, explained in plain English.
body:
Ever watched a pool match and heard "he's on the hill, but the break-and-run cost him a scratch on the bank"? If it sounded like another language, you are not alone. Pool has its own friendly slang, and once you know it, every match gets easier to follow. Here is a plain-English glossary of the words you will hear most.

The basics of the table

  • Cue ball: the white ball you strike with your cue.
  • Object ball: any ball you are aiming at with the cue ball.
  • Rail (or cushion): the padded edge of the table. Balls bounce off it.
  • Pocket: one of the six holes: four corner pockets and two side pockets.
  • Diamonds: the small markers on the rails. Players use them to measure angles, especially on bank shots.
  • Head string and foot spot: the head string is the imaginary line behind which the break starts; the foot spot is where the front ball of the rack sits.

Starting a game

  • Rack: the triangle (or diamond) used to group the balls. "Racking" means setting them up, and a single game is often called a rack too. See our guide to racking the balls.
  • Break: the opening shot that scatters the rack. Learn more in our break tips.
  • Lag: a quick opening contest to decide who breaks. Both players hit a ball down the table and back, and the one closest to the head rail wins.
  • Break and run: pocketing balls after the break and clearing the whole table without the opponent getting a turn. It is the move crowds love most.

Shots and shot-making

  • Cut shot: a shot where the cue ball hits the object ball off-center, sending it at an angle toward the pocket.
  • Bank shot: a shot that bounces the object ball off a rail before it reaches the pocket.
  • Combo (combination): hitting one object ball into another to pocket the second.
  • Kick shot: sending the cue ball off one or more rails first to reach an object ball it cannot hit directly.
  • Jump shot: lifting the cue ball into the air to hop over an obstacle. Always check local rules, since some places do not allow it.
  • Ghost ball: an aiming trick where you picture an invisible ball touching the object ball at the spot where your cue ball needs to be. See our ghost ball guide.

Cue ball control

  • English: side spin put on the cue ball by hitting it left or right of center.
  • Draw: hitting below center so the cue ball spins backward after contact.
  • Follow: hitting above center so the cue ball rolls forward after contact.
  • Stun: a center-ball hit that stops the cue ball's forward spin so it travels at an angle after contact.
  • Position play: planning where the cue ball ends up so the next shot is easy. It is the biggest difference between beginners and strong players.

Strategy and turns

  • Safety: a defensive shot that leaves your opponent with a hard or impossible next shot instead of trying to pocket a ball.
  • Snooker (or "being snookered"): when the cue ball is blocked from the ball you need to hit. In many pool games, if you cannot hit your ball directly, you must use a rail.
  • Scratch: pocketing the cue ball. In most games this is a foul.
  • Foul and ball in hand: a foul gives the opponent the chance to place the cue ball anywhere. Our fouls guide explains the common ones.
  • Run out: finishing a rack once you have started shooting.
  • Sandbag: deliberately playing worse than you can. It is not considered sporting.

Games and match talk

  • Race to (number): the match format. In a "race to 7," the first player to win seven racks wins the match.
  • On the hill: one rack away from winning the match.
  • Handicap or spot: a head start given to a weaker player so a match feels fair.
  • Call shot: a rule where you announce which ball and pocket you are aiming for. Many leagues use this in 8-ball.
  • Diamond rack: the shape used for 9-ball, with the 1 ball at the front and the 9 ball in the center. See 9-ball rules.

Handy tips for using the new words

Learning a few terms at a time works best. Try picking five from this list and listening for them the next time you watch a match or play at your local room. You can find upcoming events on our tournaments page or the pool calendar, and our guides go deeper on rules and technique.

Words can vary a little by region and by league, so if you are heading into a new league or bar room, a quick question about house rules is always welcome. Most players love to explain the game.

Quick quiz

Which of these means "one rack from winning"? If you said on the hill, you are already talking like a regular. Share the one term you did not know before in the comments on our Facebook Page, and keep practicing.
